mentions.text:
$INDI I'm long.

Indie Semiconductor is a ~$920m company in Aliso Viejo, California. They make the silicon that lets a machine see: image signal processors and radar chips for cars.

An ISP is their largest business. When a camera captures a frame, what it actually produces is a spreadsheet of brightness values, not a picture. Something has to reconstruct color, fuse multiple exposures so the pedestrian in a tunnel shadow doesn't vanish against sunlit tarmac outside, undistort a wide-angle lens, and finish it all in under thirty milliseconds, thirty times a second, on every camera in the vehicle. They also do automotive radar, the kind that sees through fog and rain when the camera can't.

Boring, right? Then this happened.

Robot companies came to them.

They went looking for a chip that could handle several camera feeds at once, in real time, on a battery, already proven reliable at scale. They found indie's automotive parts in a distributor's catalog and just bought them.

No robotics division. No robotics product. Not a dollar spent chasing a robotics customer. The orders showed up anyway.

Q2 turned that into real design wins at Unitree and Agibot. Both confirmed by the company.

@karpathy said the early Optimus once thought it was a car, because it ran the same computer, the same cameras and the same algorithms. Tesla runs eight autopilot-grade cameras on Optimus and an FSD-derived computer.

The robot and the car are the same perception problem.

Automotive spent fifteen years and enormous money building cameras that work at tunnel exits, radar that sees through fog, and processors that decide in thirty milliseconds, all qualified to survive twenty years of vibration and never fail in a way that hurts someone. Regulators forced them to. Nobody is paying that bill twice.

The part I, an AI bull, care the most about:

The iND880 processes a camera feed without a separate memory chip. Rolling window of scan lines, memory on the die, never holds a full frame. For years that was minor. One fewer component, a bit less power.

I've spent this year on the NAND and DRAM shortage from the supply side. This is the same shortage from the other end. When memory is scarce, a chip that removes the need for a memory chip stops being a cost saving and becomes the reason a line keeps running.

That's not only what made me interested in this company. That is also the CEO's take:

"In many cases, our customers are unable to source memory at all and using the 880 allows them to alleviate line-down situations."

The iND881 adds local AI so the camera identifies objects before sending anything upstream. The ams OSRAM image sensor acquisition would add the sensor itself. 

The Financials: Q2 reported August 7

Revenue $64.0m, +24% YoY, $2m above the midpoint. Core $36m, up 5% sequentially. Wuxi $28m. Non-GAAP operating loss narrowed to $8.9m from $14.5m. Cash $149m, down $35.7m on the quarter.

Q3 guided to $70m at the midpoint. Core $40m, Wuxi $30m. 30% YoY growth, accelerating.

Three things that decide the outcome:

+ Stock comp is 28% of revenue. $17.9m in Q2, up from $14.8m. That's the entire gap between the $8.9m non-GAAP loss everyone quotes and the $35.1m GAAP loss. Every "progress toward profitability" headline is non-GAAP. Dilution here is structural.

+ Cash runway is about four quarters at the current burn. The Wuxi divestiture brings $135m and roughly doubles it to eight. It's subject to Chinese regulatory approval, in this trade environment. That's not a nice-to-have, that's the balance sheet.

+ Breakeven needs core revenue up about 46%. Post-Wuxi opex around $33m. At 57% core gross margin, breakeven core revenue is roughly $58m against $40m guided this quarter. At 30% growth, call it 18 months if nothing slips.

Let's see how this plays out in the future, but I'm liking what I'm seeing.

Small money bet for now until further developments but at todays price at 3.7 I'm liking it A LOT.

Bullish $INDI ⚡️

mentions.text:
$INDI up +6% on the day, and the more I dig into it the more I like it. What @CKCapitalxx  found digging through the filings is the kind of thing you can't unsee once you've seen it.

Indie is five companies reported as one.

On the surface it's an automotive chip maker. Image signal processors and radar, the silicon that turns a camera's raw sensor data into something a car can act on in under thirty milliseconds. 

But per CK's deep dive, underneath that one segment sit four more that never get named on an earnings call:

Industrial radar, out of Germany. Not automotive. 

This is radar that stops cranes crushing people, tracks containers at ports, runs telemetry on locomotives. And the detail that makes it huge for me.

It's certified to the European machine-safety standard. 

That is the exact certification a machine needs to operate next to a human. Which is to say, the exact certification a humanoid robot needs. It's a robotics moat if you look at it from another angle.

Photonics, out of Switzerland. Light sources for fiber-optic gyroscopes, which is how aircraft and defense systems navigate when GPS is jammed.

A quantum laser. A specific wavelength whose only real buyer is someone building a quantum computer.

Plus the Chinese subsidiary everyone treats as a drag on the accounts.

Four brand names, several countries, one company.

Nobody models them separately because indie doesn't break them out. 

CK did the work of pulling them apart, and the picture that emerges is a company being valued as a single-product automotive supplier while quietly holding a portfolio of businesses in radar, photonics, defense-adjacent navigation, and quantum.

The robot thesis, that automotive perception transfers to humanoids, is real and I believe it. But it treats indie as a one-trick chip company that got lucky with robotics inbound. 

Per CK this is already a multi-domain sensing company, and the market is paying for one domain.

At roughly a $920m market cap, you're buying the automotive business and getting radar, photonics, and a quantum laser thrown in for free, along with the robotics optionality.

The risk is still really big when playing a name like this, so size it as the binary risk/reward that it is.
